steps.name: The Four Risk Tiers
steps.description:
The EU AI Act takes a risk-based approach that is commonly described as four risk tiers, and the classification determines everything that follows:
  • Unacceptable Risk (Banned) - AI practices that are prohibited by Article 5. They cannot be placed on the market, put into service or used in the EU, apart from the narrow exceptions Article 5 sets out.
  • High Risk - AI systems in sensitive areas like employment, credit scoring, and law enforcement. Permitted, but subject to strict compliance obligations.
  • Limited Risk - AI systems that interact with people. The main obligation is transparency - users must know they are dealing with AI.
  • Minimal Risk - The vast majority of AI systems. No specific obligations beyond general ones such as AI literacy.

steps.name: Real Teeth, Real Consequences
steps.description:
The EU AI Act has real teeth. Three penalty tiers, enforcement bodies at EU and national level, and the power to suspend AI systems. This is not a paper regulation - it is actively enforced.

Understanding penalties and enforcement helps you prioritize compliance efforts and respond correctly to inquiries. In this exercise, you will review the penalty structure, analyze enforcement case studies, and prepare for a regulatory inquiry.

Conformity assessment = the provider's pre-market review against EU AI Act requirements. The authority will demand both.

Alice,

This morning we received a preliminary inquiry from the national market surveillance authority about EuroTech's AI systems — a formal regulatory action under the EU AI Act.

Key details:
  • 30 days to respond with complete documentation
  • Covers all AI systems deployed across our EU operations
  • They want risk classifications, conformity assessments, FRIAs, and human oversight records
  • Incorrect, incomplete or misleading responses are a separate violation
Before we assemble the response, review the EU AI Act penalty structure so you understand the stakes:

steps.name: Penalty Tiers Reference

highlighterTexts: The authority wants risk classifications, conformity assessments, FRIAs, and human oversight records — the core artefacts of high-risk AI compliance. If EuroTech does not have them, there is nothing to send.

Incorrect, incomplete or misleading responses are themselves a separate violation. That penalty compounds on top of penalties for the underlying non-compliance — understand the tiers before you respond.
The EU AI Act uses a three-tier penalty structure. The severity of the violation determines which tier applies - and the fines scale with company size.
For SMEs and startups, penalties are proportionate to size. But for large organizations like EuroTech, the percentages of global annual turnover can translate to hundreds of millions.

Fines are only one tool. Authorities can also suspend a non-compliant AI system, force market withdrawal, and publicly disclose the violation — the reputational hit often outweighs the financial penalty.

Who is fined. The Act's fines land on the organisation, the operator, not on individual staff. An employee who knowingly misleads an authority can still face disciplinary action and, in many countries, national law.
For SME partners and startups in EuroTech's supply chain, penalties are capped at the lower of the fixed amount or the percentage of turnover — the opposite of how large companies are treated.
Proportionality is not an exemption. SMEs still owe full compliance; only the size of the financial penalty is scaled.

steps.description:
Now that Alice understands the penalty landscape, she must prepare the documentation for the authority's inquiry. The 30-day deadline means everything must be in order. The authority expects:
  • AI systems registry - Complete inventory of all deployed AI systems with risk classifications. The Act does not require one by name, but you cannot answer an inquiry like this without it
  • Conformity assessments - Documentation proving high-risk systems meet requirements
  • Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments - FRIAs for the high-risk deployments Article 27 covers, such as credit scoring
  • Human oversight records - Evidence of effective human supervision
  • Incident reports - Any serious incidents and their outcomes
  • Data governance records - Training data documentation, bias testing, quality controls
This is why governance matters. If you do not have these records, you cannot respond to an inquiry - and failing to respond is itself a violation. The Act's fines land on the organisation, the operator, not on individual staff. That does not make an inquiry only the company's problem. Key points:
  • Giving an authority incorrect or misleading information is a violation of its own (Tier 3), on top of whatever it was meant to hide
  • Employees who knowingly falsify or withhold documentation can face disciplinary action, and in many countries national law adds its own penalties
  • A manager's instruction does not make a misleading answer acceptable: raise it with compliance or legal instead
Compliance is everyone's responsibility, not just the compliance department's.

steps.name: Articles 9, 10 and 26: Bias Testing and Monitoring
steps.description:
The EU AI Act requires high-risk AI systems to be tested for bias - and the requirement goes deeper than checking for obvious discrimination. AI bias often hides in proxy variables: features that appear neutral but correlate with protected characteristics.
  • Postal code can correlate with ethnicity or socioeconomic background.
  • University name can correlate with socioeconomic status and access to opportunity.
  • Employment gaps can disproportionately affect specific demographics.
Biased AI outputs can constitute illegal discrimination even when the bias is unintentional. Providers must examine their data for bias (Article 10) and test high-risk systems before release (Article 9). Deployers must monitor them in use, and when they have reason to consider that use may present a risk, suspend the system and inform the provider or distributor and the market surveillance authority (Article 26(5)).

steps.description:
The investigation reveals the root cause. Two features dominate the screening decisions: "university ranking" (weight: 0.34) and "postal code" (weight: 0.28). Postal code shows a 0.72 correlation with Group C membership - meaning the AI is effectively using location as a proxy for demographic group membership.

Alice examines the second failing metric. The Equalized Odds Gap measures whether the AI treats equally qualified candidates equally regardless of group membership. A gap of 0.31 (threshold: 0.15) confirms that even among candidates with identical qualifications - same experience, same skills, same certifications - advancement rates differ significantly by group. The bias is systemic, not explained by qualification differences.

steps.name: Article 10: Data Governance
steps.description:
Article 10 of the EU AI Act establishes data governance requirements for high-risk AI systems. Training, validation, and testing data must meet strict quality criteria:
  • Data must be relevant to the task the AI system is designed to perform.
  • Data must be sufficiently representative of the population the model will serve, including the geographic and behavioural setting where it will be used.
  • Data must be as free of errors as possible and complete in view of the intended purpose.
  • Data governance practices must address potential biases that could lead to discriminatory outcomes.
Poor data leads to biased AI, and biased AI leads to legal liability. Data governance is not a best practice under the EU AI Act - it is a legal obligation.

steps.name: Article 73: Serious Incident Reporting
steps.description:
Under Article 73 of the EU AI Act, providers of high-risk AI systems must report "serious incidents" to the relevant market surveillance authority, and deployers must inform the provider and the authority (Article 26(5)). Article 3(49) defines a serious incident as an incident or malfunctioning that directly or indirectly leads to death or serious harm to health, a serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure, an infringement of obligations under Union law protecting fundamental rights, or serious harm to property or the environment.

Reporting timelines are strict, and providers and deployers have distinct obligations. Today, one of your company's AI systems has triggered exactly this scenario.

steps.name: Reporting Timelines
steps.description:
The report has been submitted internally. Now, the legal timeline begins. Under Article 73, providers of high-risk AI systems must report serious incidents to the market surveillance authority:
  • Immediately after the provider has established a causal link, or the reasonable likelihood of one, between the AI system and the incident
  • No later than 15 days after the provider or, where applicable, the deployer becomes aware of the serious incident
  • Sooner in the gravest cases: no later than 2 days for a widespread infringement or a serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure, and no later than 10 days if a person has died
Deployers must inform the provider immediately, and then the market surveillance authority (Article 26(5)). Both providers and deployers must cooperate fully with any subsequent investigation by the authorities. SynapseAI deploys OnboardAI but did not build it - the provider is OnboardAI's vendor. SynapseAI must notify them immediately so they can fulfill their own reporting obligations.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.description:
Alice handled this incident correctly by refusing the vendor's request to delay reporting. Here are the key principles for AI incident reporting under the EU AI Act:
  • Report on time: Providers must report within 15 days of becoming aware, and sooner in the gravest cases: 2 days for a widespread infringement or critical infrastructure disruption, 10 days if someone has died. Deployers must inform the provider immediately, then the authority. Missing these deadlines creates additional legal liability.
  • Contain first, then investigate: Stop the ongoing harm immediately. Root cause analysis and formal reporting come after containment, not before.
  • Never delay because a vendor asks you to: The reporting obligation exists regardless of whether the vendor wants to "fix it first." Delaying a report does not make the obligation disappear - it adds an obstruction risk.
  • The obligation exists regardless of intent: Whether the discrimination was caused by a bug, a data pipeline error, or a design flaw does not matter. The harm to 230 people and the breach of fundamental rights is what triggers the reporting requirement.
  • Cooperate with authorities: Obstruction or non-cooperation makes the consequences significantly worse for everyone involved.
  • Document everything: From the moment you become aware of the incident, keep detailed records. Timestamps, data, decisions, and communications all become part of the official record.

steps.name: Article 50: Transparency Obligations
steps.description:
Article 50 of the EU AI Act sets transparency duties that apply whatever an AI system's risk class:
  • Chatbots must be designed so people know they are dealing with AI, unless it is obvious. That duty sits with the provider that builds them.
  • Synthetic content generated by AI must be marked by the provider in a machine-readable way, so it can be detected as AI-made.
  • Deep fakes must be disclosed by the deployer that publishes them: AI-made or altered images, audio or video that resemble real people, places, objects or events and could pass for authentic. Evident satire or art still discloses, in a way that does not spoil it.
  • AI text published to inform the public must be disclosed too, unless a person reviewed it and someone holds editorial responsibility.
These are legal requirements, not good practice, and breaching them can be fined.

steps.name: Article 27: Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment
steps.note: FRIA = Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (EU AI Act Article 27). DPIA = Data Protection Impact Assessment (GDPR Article 35). Different scope: one does not replace the other.
steps.description:
Article 27 of the EU AI Act requires certain deployers of high-risk AI systems (public bodies, private entities providing public services, and deployers of credit-scoring or life and health insurance AI) to conduct a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment before first use. A social housing benefit system that CivicTech runs on behalf of municipal councils is in scope: CivicTech provides a public service by deciding eligibility for public assistance (Annex III 5(a)), so Article 27 makes it a deployer that must complete the FRIA. A FRIA examines how the AI system might affect fundamental rights - dignity, non-discrimination, privacy, freedom of expression, and the right to an effective remedy.

A FRIA differs from a GDPR Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA). While a DPIA focuses solely on data protection risks, a FRIA covers all fundamental rights. Both assessments may be required for the same system, and they can be conducted together.

steps.name: Section 5: Monitoring Plan
steps.description:
A FRIA is a living document.

Article 27(2) requires an update whenever an element of the assessment (such as the people affected, the risks or the mitigation measures) has changed or is no longer up to date, for instance after a new model, new data or a wider scope. A scheduled annual review on top of that is good practice.

Escalation paths must be defined so rights-affecting incidents trigger immediate review.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.description: FRIAs are mandatory for in-scope deployers before first use Public bodies, providers of public services, and deployers of credit-scoring or life and health insurance AI must complete a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment before a high-risk system is used for the first time. For them it is a legal obligation under Article 27, not an optional best practice. FRIAs and DPIAs serve different purposes A FRIA covers all fundamental rights - non-discrimination, dignity, privacy, effective remedy, freedom of expression. A DPIA under GDPR focuses only on data protection. Both may be required for the same AI system and can be conducted together, but one does not replace the other. FRIAs must be proportionate and specific The assessment must be tailored to the specific AI system and its deployment context. A social housing eligibility system affects different rights than a content moderation system. Results go to the market surveillance authority Once the assessment is done, the deployer notifies the market surveillance authority of its results (Article 27(3)). FRIAs are living documents A FRIA must be updated whenever an element of it has changed or is no longer up to date - for example after new data sources, an expanded scope or modified algorithms. A scheduled annual review on top of that is good practice.

steps.name: High-Risk AI Requirements
steps.description:
High-risk AI systems have the strictest obligations under the EU AI Act. The system itself must meet requirements across seven areas (Articles 9-15), and it is the provider's job to meet them (Article 16). As the deployer, you should see the provider's evidence of each before use, then meet your own duties under Article 26:
  • Risk management - Identify and mitigate risks throughout the system lifecycle
  • Data governance - Ensure training data is relevant, representative, and free from bias
  • Technical documentation - Maintain detailed documentation of the system's design and function
  • Record-keeping - Enable audit trails and automatic logging
  • Transparency - Provide clear information and instructions for use to deployers
  • Human oversight - Ensure humans can effectively supervise the system
  • Accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity - Meet performance and security standards
This exercise walks through a deployer's review of a real deployment: checking the provider's evidence and closing the gaps that are yours.

steps.description:
High-risk AI deployment is not just "install and configure." It is a structured compliance process with ongoing obligations. The seven requirement areas are not checkboxes to rush through - they protect people affected by AI decisions. Key takeaways:

steps.name: Articles 14 and 26: Human Oversight
steps.description:
The EU AI Act requires that high-risk AI systems have meaningful human oversight. Articles 14 and 26 point to three things a human reviewer needs for meaningful oversight:
  • You must be competent - trained to understand the AI system's capabilities and limitations.
  • You must have authority to override the AI's decisions when warranted.
  • You should exercise independent judgment on each case, not simply confirm what the AI recommends.
The primary threat to meaningful oversight is automation bias - the tendency to over-rely on AI recommendations because they seem authoritative. The EU AI Act expects the people overseeing the system to stay aware of this tendency (Article 14(4)(b)).

Scoring business loans is not itself on the Annex III high-risk list, which covers the creditworthiness of individuals (point 5(b)). Atlas applies the Article 14 and 26 standard to every credit decision anyway, as company policy.

steps.name: Provider vs. Deployer
steps.note: Conformity assessment = the formal review verifying an AI system meets EU AI Act requirements before going on the market. CE marking = the visible mark applied after passing that assessment (the same EU mark on toys, electronics, and medical devices).
steps.description:

  • Deployer - The company that uses an AI system under its own authority. Responsible for human oversight, monitoring, keeping logs, informing the people affected, and incident reporting. steps.name: Two Frameworks, One AI System
steps.description:
The EU AI Act and GDPR overlap significantly when AI systems process personal data. Any AI system that handles personal data is covered by GDPR, and by the EU AI Act as well when it falls within its scope, as the triage system in this exercise does.
  • GDPR lawful basis - a valid legal ground is required for processing personal data.
  • GDPR Article 22 - individuals have the right not to be subject to purely automated decisions with significant effects.
  • DPIA requirements - a Data Protection Impact Assessment may be required under GDPR for high-risk processing.
  • Data minimization - only data necessary for the specific purpose may be processed.
These are independent legal frameworks with their own enforcement mechanisms, but they create overlapping obligations for AI systems that handle personal data.

steps.name: Lawful Basis for Health Data
steps.description:
The triage system processes health data, which is a special category under GDPR Article 9. Standard processing grounds like legitimate interest are not sufficient for health data. The Article 9(2) conditions that fit this case are:
  • Explicit consent (GDPR Art. 9(2)(a)) - the patient gives explicit, informed consent to the processing of their health data by the AI system.
  • Necessary for medical treatment or diagnosis (GDPR Art. 9(2)(h)) - the processing is necessary for healthcare purposes and is carried out by a health professional or someone subject to professional secrecy obligations.
Legitimate interest alone is never sufficient for processing health data under GDPR. Organizations must identify a valid Article 9(2) condition in addition to an Article 6 lawful basis.

For this healthcare AI system, two separate impact assessments may be required:
  • DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment) - required under GDPR when processing is likely to result in a high risk to individuals' rights. Focuses specifically on data protection risks: how personal data is collected, stored, processed, and protected.
  • FRIA (Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment) - required under EU AI Act Article 27 before high-risk AI is used by public bodies, providers of public services such as healthcare, or deployers of credit-scoring or life and health insurance AI. Covers all fundamental rights more broadly: non-discrimination, dignity, access to healthcare, freedom, and the right to an effective remedy.
These assessments serve different legal purposes and have different scopes. They can be conducted together as a combined exercise, but each must meet the requirements of its respective regulation.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.description:
Here is what to remember when AI systems process personal data:
  • Dual compliance often applies: AI systems that process personal data are always covered by GDPR, and by the EU AI Act as well when they fall within its scope, as this triage system does. These are independent frameworks with separate enforcement.
  • Human oversight serves both frameworks: GDPR Article 22 gives people a right not to be subject to purely automated decisions, with safeguards such as human intervention (Article 22(3)), while EU AI Act Article 14 requires high-risk systems to be designed for effective human oversight. The legal reasons differ. They are complementary, not substitutes.
  • Data minimization applies even when more data would help: Processing more data than necessary violates GDPR regardless of whether it improves AI performance.
  • Privacy notices must satisfy both frameworks: GDPR requires transparency about data processing; the EU AI Act requires transparency about AI system usage. Both can be addressed in a single notice.
  • Both DPIA and FRIA may be required: A DPIA focuses on data protection risks; a FRIA covers all fundamental rights. They serve different purposes even when conducted together.
  • Patients have rights under both: GDPR gives access to information (Articles 13-15) and human intervention in purely automated decisions (Article 22(3)); the EU AI Act adds a right to an explanation of high-risk AI decisions (Article 86).

steps.name: Articles 51-56: General-Purpose AI
steps.note: FLOPs = floating-point operations, the standard measure of computational work used to train an AI model. The 10^25 FLOPs threshold roughly captures today's frontier models.
steps.description:
The EU AI Act introduces a dedicated framework for General-Purpose AI (GPAI) models under Articles 51-56. GPAI models are AI models trained on broad data that can perform a wide range of tasks - large language models are the primary example.
  • GPAI providers must supply technical documentation (including the model's energy consumption), comply with EU copyright law, and publish a sufficiently detailed summary of their training data.
  • Systemic risk GPAI - models trained with compute exceeding 10^25 FLOPs, or designated by the AI Office - have additional obligations including adversarial testing (red-teaming), systemic risk assessment and mitigation, incident reporting, and cybersecurity measures.
These obligations apply to the model provider. But downstream companies building products on GPAI models inherit their own set of responsibilities.

Items badged Systemic Risk Only stack on top once the threshold is crossed: adversarial testing, systemic risk mitigation, incident reporting, and cybersecurity. Titan-7's model card has no adversarial testing results.

steps.name: Downstream Obligations and Copyright
steps.description: When NovaMind builds a customer support platform on a GPAI model, the resulting system may be classified independently under the EU AI Act's risk framework. A general customer FAQ bot is likely limited risk (transparency only). But if the system makes decisions affecting customer access to services, credit, or insurance, it could be high-risk -- triggering conformity assessment, human oversight, and incident reporting. NovaMind must assess this independently; the GPAI provider's obligations do not cover the downstream provider's risk classification. Copyright compliance also flows through the value chain. GPAI providers must comply with EU copyright law, including the text and data mining opt-out (Article 4, DSM Directive). If a GPAI model generates content resembling copyrighted material and NovaMind serves it to customers, both the provider and NovaMind may face liability. Before building on any GPAI model, verify the provider's copyright compliance documentation and consider content filtering safeguards.

steps.name: The Absolute Red Lines
steps.description:
Article 5 of the EU AI Act defines certain AI practices that are outright banned in the EU. No workarounds. Penalties for prohibited practices are the highest tier under the Act: up to 35 million euros or 7% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher. The eight categories of prohibited AI under Article 5(1) are:
  • (a) Manipulative or deceptive AI techniques that materially distort behavior and cause or are likely to cause significant harm
  • (b) AI exploiting vulnerabilities of specific groups (age, disability, social or economic situation) to materially distort behavior and cause significant harm
  • (c) Social scoring - evaluating or classifying people over time on social behavior or personal traits, leading to detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts or treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate
  • (d) Predicting that a person will commit a crime based solely on profiling or personality traits
  • (e) Untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV to build facial recognition databases
  • (f) Emotion recognition in workplace and educational settings (except for medical or safety reasons)
  • (g) Biometric categorization to infer sensitive attributes (race, political opinions, sexual orientation)
  • (h) Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, with three narrow exceptions: searching for victims of abduction, trafficking or missing persons; preventing a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or a terrorist attack; and locating suspects of listed serious crimes

Customers with low scores get routed to slower support queues. Using AI-generated scores to treat people detrimentally - in this case, degraded service quality - is exactly what Article 5(1)(c) prohibits.

steps.name: Understanding Social Scoring
steps.description: This is social scoring, prohibited under Article 5(1)(c). Using AI to evaluate people based on their social behavior or personal characteristics - and then using those scores to treat them detrimentally - is banned. Returns and support tickets on their own are ordinary business data. What crosses the line is scoring customers on their social media activity, behaviour from an unrelated context, and using that score to push them into slower support: detrimental treatment in a context unrelated to where the data came from, and also unjustified and out of proportion. Either condition on its own is enough. The prohibition applies regardless of whether the scoring happens to existing customers or prospective ones.
